problemText: Earth is built in three main layers. Starting at the surface and moving down toward the center of the planet, which layer comes first?
choices: The crust
The mantle
The core
The metal layer
hints: Think about which layer is closest to the ground where people live.
The crust is described as the outermost layer, right under the ground and ocean floor.

problemText: A geologist is studying a rock sample taken from a deep mine shaft. The sample is solid rock and was obtained by drilling down from Earth's surface. Based on these two facts alone, which layer must this sample come from?
choices: The mantle, because it is solid rock that sits between the surface and the center
The crust, because it is the only layer people have ever drilled into directly
The core, because it is solid and sits deeper than any mine can reach
Either the mantle or the core, since both are deeper than the crust
hints: Nobody has ever drilled anywhere close to the mantle or core through any drilling project.
The crust is the thinnest layer and the only one people have reached directly by digging or drilling.

problemText: Earth's three layers can be identified by where they sit or by what they are made of. The mantle is solid rock, but the core is made mostly of metal instead. If you learn that a particular layer inside Earth is made of metal, which layer have you identified?
choices: The crust
The mantle
The core
The layer closest to the surface
hints: The crust and mantle are both made of rock, not metal.
Only one layer in Earth's three-layer model has a different composition from the other two.

problemText: A scientist describes a layer of Earth as follows: it sits between the surface and the very center of the planet, it is made of solid rock, and it fills more space inside Earth than the other two layers combined. Which layer matches all three of these descriptions, and why does this description rule out the other two layers?
choices: The crust, because it sits at the surface and is the thinnest layer, so it fails both the position test and the size test
Both the crust and the mantle, since both are made of solid rock and would satisfy the material requirement
The core, because it is made of metal and sits at Earth's very center, which fails the position requirement of being between the surface and center
The mantle, because it is the only layer that sits in the middle and fills most of Earth's inside
hints: The description says the layer sits between the surface and center — which position rules out both the crust and the core?
The mantle is the only layer described as filling most of the space inside Earth.

problemText: Two clues are given about a layer inside Earth: it is the thinnest of the three layers, and nobody has ever drilled into it from the surface during any drilling project. Explain why these two clues together must point to the crust and cannot point to either the mantle or the core.
choices: The crust is thinnest and sits closest to the surface, while the mantle and core sit below it where drills cannot reach
The mantle and core are both made of different materials, so they are easier to drill through than rock
The mantle fills most of Earth's inside, and the core is hotter, so both are too large to be the thinnest layer
The crust is the only layer made of rock, while the mantle and core are made of materials that block drilling
hints: If a layer sits deeper inside Earth, would it be easier or harder for people to reach it by drilling from the surface?
The crust is the only layer that sits right under the ground and ocean floor, making it reachable by drilling.

problemText: A student reads this description of an unknown layer: 'This layer sits farther from Earth's surface than the crust does, but not as far as the very center. It is solid rock and extremely hot.' The student then reasons: 'Since this layer is solid rock, it could be either the crust or the mantle. I need one more clue to decide between them.' Is the student's reasoning correct, and why or why not? Which layer is actually being described?
choices: Yes, the student is correct; the description points to the crust because it mentions being extremely hot, which is a property unique to the outermost layer
No, the student is wrong; the description of position — farther from the surface than the crust but not at the center — already rules out the crust and points only to the mantle
Yes, the student is correct; being solid rock narrows it to two layers, and being extremely hot is the clue that settles it between the crust and mantle
No, the student is wrong; because only the core is extremely hot, so the description cannot apply to either the crust or the mantle at all
hints: The position described is 'farther from the surface than the crust but not at the center.' Does this position match the crust, the mantle, or the core?
The crust is the layer closest to the surface; if something sits farther from the surface than the crust, it cannot be the crust.

problemText: A solid rock sits on a mountainside for decades. Freezing water gets into a crack in the rock, expands, and pushes the crack wider. The small pieces that break free stay right there in the same crack. What is the name of the process that breaks the rock apart in the place where it already sits?
choices: Sediment
Erosion
Deposition
Weathering
hints: The key word in the question is 'stays right there' — nothing moves anywhere.
Look for the process that breaks something apart without carrying it away.

problemText: A river is flowing fast after heavy rain. Loose pebbles that sat on the riverbed have been picked up by the flowing water. The pebbles are tumbling along the river bottom right now, moving downstream with the current. The river is still flowing hard and the pebbles are still moving. Which process is happening at this moment?
choices: Erosion, because the loose pebbles are being carried from one place toward another
Weathering, because water is breaking the pebbles into smaller pieces as they tumble
Deposition, because the pebbles are being transported by the flowing water downstream
Weathering, because the pebbles are loose and being moved by the river current
hints: The question says the pebbles are 'still moving' right now — so focus on what is happening at this exact moment, not what might happen later.
Erosion is the process of carrying something that is already loose. Ask yourself: are the pebbles being carried?

problemText: A patch of bare soil sits on a hillside. For months, the sun beats down on it, drying it out, and wind carries away tiny grains of dried soil. The dried grains blow off the patch and scatter across a neighboring yard. The original patch stays in the same location on the hillside the whole time. Which process describes what the wind is doing to the soil grains as it carries them away?
choices: Weathering, because the sun and wind are breaking the soil grains into smaller particles
Erosion, because wind is carrying loose soil grains from one place to another
Deposition, because the wind is transporting the soil grains to the neighboring yard
Weathering, because the soil grains are being broken apart by the drying process
hints: The test for erosion is: is an already-loose piece on the move? The soil grains were already loose before the wind picked them up.
Pay attention to the fact that the grains are being 'carried away' from the patch to a different location.

problemText: A marble statue stands in a park. Rain seeps into a small crack in the marble and freezes each winter, making the crack spread a tiny bit wider. After many winters, loose marble chips finally break free from around the crack. A hard rainstorm washes these chips down the path and deposits them in a drainage ditch fifty meters away. Which two of the three processes happen in this story, and in what order?
choices: Deposition first, then erosion, because the chips start in the ditch and end in the crack
Erosion first, then weathering, because the rain moves things before the frost breaks them apart
Weathering first, then erosion, because the frost widens the crack and then rain washes the chips away
Weathering only, because the chips never leave the statue
hints: Remember the rule: weathering must happen before erosion, because nothing can be carried away until it has been broken loose first.
Look for the moment when something breaks apart in place (that is weathering), and then find when a loose piece is carried somewhere else (that is erosion).

problemText: A student is trying to identify a process but makes an error. She sees a strong ocean wave crashing against a cliff. Sand and rock debris are swirling in the foam and churning water right against the cliff face. She says, 'The wave is weathering the cliff because it is breaking up the sand and rock.' Explain why her reasoning is wrong, and identify which process is actually happening.
choices: She is wrong because the sand and rock are not actually being moved anywhere, so nothing but weathering is occurring at the cliff
She is wrong because waves cannot weather anything; only freezing water trapped in cracks can weather rock through ice expansion
She is right about weathering happening, but she missed that erosion is also occurring when the wave carries loose material away from the cliff
She is wrong because weathering only happens when material breaks apart while staying in the same place; the wave is actually causing erosion, since it is carrying loose material away from the cliff
hints: The key to weathering is that nothing moves. But the sand and rock are 'swirling' and 'churning' — so are they staying in one place?
Erosion is the carrying of material that is already loose. The wave is carrying loose sand and rock, so that fits the test for erosion, not weathering.

problemText: A boulder has sat on a mountainside for years. Frost, wind, and rain gradually break it into smaller and smaller chunks over time, but all the chunks stay piled in roughly the same spot. Then, during a heavy storm, a landslide pushes the chunks down the slope and scatters them across a flat valley floor below. Years later, a slow stream moves some of those chunks a short distance downstream and leaves them in a new pile when the stream gets shallow and slows down. Describe which processes happen in this story and explain why you can identify each one, but also note which process does NOT happen anywhere in the story.
choices: Weathering breaks the boulder into chunks on the mountainside; erosion scatters them in the landslide and moves them in the stream; deposition drops them in the valley and in the new pile. All three processes happen.
Only erosion and deposition happen. The boulder breaks into chunks due to frost and rain, but that is natural breakdown, not weathering, because weathering only occurs near water.
Weathering, erosion, and deposition all occur, but deposition happens twice — first when the landslide stops the chunks in the valley, and second when the stream stops them in the new pile.

Erosion happens twice (in the landslide and the stream) and deposition happens once (in the new stream pile), but weathering does not happen because breaking rocks into chunks is not weathering if the chunks stay in roughly the same place.
hints: Apply the test for each process separately. Ask: (1) Does something break apart in place? (2) Is something already loose and being carried? (3) Does something that was moving come to rest in a new spot?

Notice that all three processes can involve the same material in sequence: weathering breaks it apart, erosion carries it, and deposition drops it. The landslide and the stream are both forces that carry loose material, so they both cause erosion.

problemText: A rock formed when magma cooled and hardened into solid rock deep underground. Which rock type is this?
choices: Metamorphic rock
Sedimentary rock
Igneous rock
Magma rock
hints: The definition of igneous rock starts with melted rock cooling and hardening.
Magma is the name for melted rock, so cooling magma makes a specific rock type.

problemText: Two rocks are found in the same mountain. One rock looks pink and has large crystals. The other rock is gray and has tiny crystals. A geologist says both are igneous rocks. How is this possible if they look so different?
choices: They look different because they formed in different ways, so one must be sedimentary rock instead of igneous.
The geologist made a mistake because rocks that are the same type must always look identical in color and crystal size.
They are the same rock type only if they both have crystals, and the crystal size difference does not matter to the rock classification.
They can be the same type because rock type is decided by how it formed, not by color or crystal size.
hints: Rock type depends on the process that made it, not on appearance.
Igneous rocks can cool at different speeds, making crystals of different sizes.

problemText: A student finds a rock made of sand grains that have been pressed tightly together. The rock is hard and solid. Which rock type is this, and what must have happened over a very long time to make it solid?
choices: Sedimentary rock, because loose sand grains settled into layers and were pressed together.
Igneous rock, because sand grains were melted and then cooled.
Metamorphic rock, because sand grains were changed by intense heat and pressure.
Sedimentary rock, because the sand grains were melted deep underground.
hints: Sand grains that are pressed together fit the definition of sedimentary rock formation.
Sedimentary rock comes from loose pieces, not from melting or squeezing an existing rock.

problemText: An igneous rock is pushed deep underground where it is squeezed by intense heat and pressure for millions of years. The rock never fully melts, but it changes into a new type of rock. What type is the new rock, and why did it not become igneous rock again?
choices: Sedimentary rock, because the loose pieces of the old rock settled into a new layer and were compacted together over time.
Metamorphic rock, because an existing rock was changed by heat and pressure without melting.
Igneous rock, because intense heat always causes rock to melt and then harden again into a new igneous form.
Metamorphic rock, but it would become igneous rock instead if the temperature were raised high enough to cause complete melting.
hints: The key difference is whether the rock fully melts: full melting makes igneous, but no melting makes metamorphic.
An existing rock changed by heat and pressure without melting fits the metamorphic definition exactly.

problemText: A sedimentary rock and an igneous rock are both buried deep underground in the same location and exposed to the same intense heat and pressure for a very long time. Neither rock fully melts. What will happen to each rock, and why might the outcome be the same for both?
choices: Both will become sedimentary rock because they are buried in the same place and experience the same conditions.
The sedimentary rock will become metamorphic, but the igneous rock will stay igneous because its starting type determines its fate.
Both will become metamorphic rock because heat and pressure without full melting defines that type.
Both will become igneous rock because being buried underground causes the rocks to melt and recrystallize as new igneous material.
hints: Rock type is determined by how it was made, not what type it started as.
If an existing rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting, it becomes metamorphic no matter what type it was before.

problemText: A geologist studies a piece of metamorphic rock and predicts what might happen to it next in the rock cycle. She suggests two possible futures: Future A, where the rock is buried even deeper and melts completely, then cools and hardens; or Future B, where the rock is pushed upward and broken into loose grains that settle into a new layer and are pressed together. According to the rock cycle, which future would produce which rock type, and why does the rock cycle have no single required path that every rock must follow?
choices: Future A makes igneous rock and Future B makes metamorphic rock because what happens to rock deep underground always results in metamorphic changes rather than other transformations.
Future A makes sedimentary rock and Future B makes igneous rock because the rock must cycle through each type in the same order every time it changes forms.
Both futures make metamorphic rock because the starting material was already metamorphic and metamorphic rocks cannot be transformed into sedimentary or igneous varieties through any process.
Future A makes igneous rock and Future B makes sedimentary rock; different things happening to a rock make different types, not the rock's starting type.
hints: Trace each future: full melting plus cooling defines igneous; loose pieces settling and being pressed together defines sedimentary.
The same starting rock can become different types because what actually happens to it decides its fate, not what it used to be.

problemText: Earth's outer rocky shell is not one solid, unbroken skin. What does geology call the large slabs that make up this broken shell?
choices: Continental crusts
Tectonic plates
Plate boundaries
Rock layers
hints: The word 'tectonic' relates to the structure and movement of Earth's outer layers.
Think of the shell as broken into separate pieces, not a single piece.

problemText: A student measures that a tectonic plate moves 4 centimeters in one year. At this rate, how far would that same plate move in 1 million years?
choices: 400 kilometers
4 kilometers
40 kilometers
4,000 kilometers
hints: Convert centimeters to kilometers: there are 100,000 centimeters in 1 kilometer.
Multiply the annual movement by the number of years to find the total distance.

problemText: A geographer explains that the rock far below Earth's tectonic plates is extremely hot and can slowly change shape over millions of years, even though it remains solid. Which material does this solid rock most resemble in how it behaves?
choices: Loose sand that shifts with every vibration
Liquid lava that flows freely like water
A frozen block of ice that never bends
Very stiff putty that creeps slowly under pressure
hints: The rock is solid, not melted or liquid, so rules out options with flowing or liquid behavior.
Over enormous time spans, the solid rock can move and deform gradually, like thick paste.

problemText: Scientists found fossils of an ancient animal species only in South America and southern Africa. The same animal could not have swum across the Atlantic Ocean. Additionally, bands of rock of the same age and type were found on the east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa. What can geographers conclude from both of these pieces of evidence together?
choices: The two continents were once joined in a single landmass that later split apart
The ancient animals evolved separately on each continent in the same way
Ocean currents must have carried the animal eggs across the water long ago
The rock bands were formed at the same time but in different oceans
hints: Look for the explanation that accounts for BOTH the matching fossils AND the matching rock layers at the same time.
If the continents were separate, how would identical ancient animals and rock types end up on opposite sides of an ocean?

problemText: A geologist marks every recorded earthquake and volcano on a globe using small dots. After plotting data from around the world, the geologist notices the dots do not spread evenly across Earth's surface. Instead, they form long bands in certain regions, while vast areas in the middle of continents and oceans have almost no marks. What does this pattern tell us about the relationship between earthquakes, volcanoes, and tectonic plates?
choices: Earthquakes and volcanoes are more common in the Southern Hemisphere than the Northern Hemisphere
Earthquakes and volcanoes occur mostly where tectonic plates meet each other
The center of each continent is geologically unstable and prone to sudden eruptions
Volcanoes and earthquakes happen randomly and cannot be predicted by plate location
hints: The bands of marks trace the edges and boundaries where different plates join.
The middle of a plate is described as a quiet place, while the rim is where things happen.

problemText: A student reads in an old newspaper article from 1924 that the continents are floating on a boiling ocean of liquid rock beneath Earth's surface, and that because the continents move so quickly, maps would need to be redrawn every few years to stay accurate. The student then reviews what modern geologists know about plate tectonics. How many separate scientific errors does the old article contain, and what is correct in modern understanding?
choices: Two errors: continents do not move at all, and there is no liquid rock layer anywhere beneath Earth's crust
One error: the rock is liquid, but the plates do move fast enough to require map updates every decade
Two errors: the rock below is solid (not liquid), and plates move only centimeters per year (far too slowly to redraw maps in years)
Three errors: the ocean beneath is made of magma not lava, the continents move too slowly, and earthquakes prove the plates are frozen in place
hints: Check each claim: Is the rock beneath the plates liquid or solid? Do maps need to be redrawn because of plate movement over a century?
A few centimeters per year over 100 years adds up to only a few meters — too small to see on a world map, but over millions of years it reaches hundreds of kilometers.
